pronunciation.approximation: mun-joo-SHREE — the ñ is the nasal of 'canyon'; śrī is one syllable, the 'sh' softened.
pronunciation.note: Mañjuśrī is a compound: mañju, "gentle, sweet, lovely," + śrī, "glory, splendor" (Monier-Williams) — "the Gentle Glory." His other names are a litany of the same music: Mañjughoṣa, "Gentle Voice"; Vāgīśvara, "Lord of Speech." The restoration keeps the palatal ñ, the ś, and the long ī; the ASCII "Manjushri" loses all three. Tier-1 by rule: three distinctive letters preserved.

domains.title: The Gentle Glory
domains.subtitle: The Flaming Sword, the Book on the Lotus, and the Mountain of Five Terraces
domains.lead: Mañjuśrī is the bodhisattva of transcendent wisdom: the ever-youthful prince who raises the flaming sword that cuts ignorance and bears the book of the Perfection of Wisdom on a blue lotus — the mind of every Buddha made visible as a sixteen-year-old with a blade.

cards.name: The Flaming Sword
cards.desc: The khadga that does not wound but severs: ignorance cut at the root, wisdom flaming at the edge.

cards.name: The Book on the Lotus
cards.desc: The Prajñāpāramitā volume resting on a blue utpala — the text the sword serves.

cards.name: The Lion Mount
cards.desc: He rides the lion of the teaching — wisdom's roar that no argument withstands.

cards.name: A Ra Pa Tsa Na
cards.desc: Oṃ A Ra Pa Tsa Na Dhīḥ — the Arapacana syllabary as mantra, recited for a sharp mind.

symbols.name: The flaming sword
symbols.meaning: Discrimination that liberates: the cut that ends confusion, not the one that starts it

symbols.name: The blue lotus and the book
symbols.meaning: Wisdom as a text to be carried and a flower that opens by itself

symbols.name: The seed syllable Dhīḥ
symbols.meaning: The sound of insight itself, traced on children's tongues in the Himalaya

mythology.lead: Mañjuśrī's mythology is the biography of wisdom itself: he appears wherever the sūtras need the hardest question asked — and answered without a flicker.

myths.title: The Debate of Non-Duality
myths.text: When the layman Vimalakīrti feigned illness to teach, every bodhisattva found an excuse not to visit — each remembered being corrected by him once. Mañjuśrī alone went, leading the whole assembly, and their exchange is the sūtra's summit: asked how a bodhisattva enters non-duality, Vimalakīrti answered Mañjuśrī's courtesy with silence, and Mañjuśrī pronounced the silence itself the teaching. It is the most famous consultation in Buddhist literature — the wisdom bodhisattva certifying that the highest truth declines to be phrased.

myths.title: The Nāga King's Daughter
myths.text: In the Lotus Sūtra's twelfth chapter, Mañjuśrī returns from the nāga palace under the sea and reports that the dragon king's daughter — eight years old — has attained full awakening. The elder Śāriputra objects on every ground the age could supply; the girl appears, offers a jewel to the Buddha, and demonstrates her enlightenment before the assembly. The chapter is Mañjuśrī's brief for the universality of awakening: wisdom, taught well, does not check credentials.

myths.title: The Sword That Drained the Lake
myths.text: Nepal's own scripture, the Svayambhū Purāṇa, makes him the valley's founder: when the Kathmandu basin was a serpent lake, Mañjuśrī came from the five-peaked mountain of the north, saw the self-existent flame — the svayambhū — floating on the waters, and with one stroke of his sword cut the gorge at Chobhar so the lake drained and people could settle. The flame remained on its hill as the Svayambhū stūpa, the valley's crown to this day. It is his iconography read as geography: the sword that opens a way for beings to live.

myths.title: Clear-and-Cool Mountain
myths.text: The Avataṃsaka Sūtra names his earthly dwelling: a mountain in the northeast called Clear-and-Cool, where he teaches amid ten thousand bodhisattvas. Chinese Buddhists identified the peak with Wǔtái shān, the five-terraced mountain of Shanxi, and made it East Asia's greatest bodhisattva pilgrimage: Tibetan lamas, Mongol khans, and Chinese emperors all climbed the terraces to meet him. Pilgrims still watch the mountain's famous halo-lights for his lion — and the mountain still answers to his name.

lore.syncretism: He is the most portable of the great bodhisattvas: Wénshū in China, Monju in Japan, 'Jam dpal in Tibet — and in Tibet his cult became inseparable from scholarship itself, Tsongkhapa venerated as his emanation and the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti, "Chanting the Names of Mañjuśrī," recited as the daily liturgy of the monasteries; Wayman's translation made the text a classic in the West. With Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi he forms the lords of the three families — wisdom, compassion, and power — the triad painted over a thousand Himalayan doorways. His sword-and-book traveled the sea routes as well: his images stand in the temples of Buddhist Java.
lore.culturalLegacy: Mañjuśrī is the patron saint of students across half the world: Himalayan children still have the syllable Dhīḥ traced on their tongues for a quick mind, and his Arapacana mantra is murmured before examinations from Ladakh to Lhasa. His iconography — sword in the right hand, book on the lotus at the left — is the universal Buddhist shorthand for the two halves of wisdom, cutting and knowing. Mount Wutai, his earthly seat, is a UNESCO landscape where a dozen languages still call on Wénshū.
lore.extendedMeditation: Mañjuśrī is the proof that clarity is a form of compassion: the sword is raised not against persons but against the fog that makes persons suffer. His youth is the point — wisdom is not the slow deposit of years but the freshness of a mind that has not agreed to be confused. He asks of every learner the one question his book and blade pose together: what are you willing to have cut, so that what remains can finally be read?

sources.name: Wayman, Chanting the Names of Mañjuśrī

lore.archaeology: His mountain is the monument: Wǔtái shān preserves the Nanchan temple (782) and the Foguang temple's East Hall (857) — the two oldest surviving timber halls in China — on the terraces pilgrims have climbed for fifteen centuries. The Kathmandu valley keeps his founding stroke in stone and water: the Chobhar gorge through which the lake drained, and the Svayambhū stūpa on its hill, eyes painted and sword remembered. His certain images emerge in the early centuries CE and multiply along the Silk Road; by the Pāla period the sword-and-book type was fixed, and it has not changed since.
